text:
Moth and Gravel. Field Note 7
Fast signals, slow eyes.

An AI narrated edition of the
published note. A place to look.

A little machine can send
numbers faster than a person can

make sense of them. Put every
arrival on a screen and the

display begins to feel busy.
Keep the latest value and

something else becomes possible.
A place to look.

The Katronic Buggies Python
telemetry dashboard makes that

choice. A receiver replaces the
current readings when a packet

arrives. The Tkinter interface
reads that shared state, draws

the gauges, and schedules its
next update 33 milliseconds

later. That interval describes
the requested pause after an

update. It does not establish a
measure measured frame rate. The

work of drawing and whatever
else the window is doing takes
time, too.

A current value needs a
condition. A value can stay on

screen after the machine has
stopped speaking. Without

another cue, the last answer can
look like the present one. The

dashboard has a small correction
for that impression. At a

refresh, it checks how long it
has been since the last packet.

Less than half a second gets
connected label. At half a

second or more, the label
becomes stale data. The gauges

still draw from the latest
packet. The number can remain

useful, but its relationship to
now has changed.

O1 at a refresh. The packet is
still recent. One fictional

refresh 0.2 seconds after
arrival, the source's label is

connected. O2 at a later
refresh. The same packet has

aged. No new packet. A fictional
refresh at 0.6 seconds, the
source's label is stale data.

One arrival, two reading
moments. The first marker is

packet arrival. The dashed line
marks the source's 0.5 second

boundary. These are schematic
examples, not a measured timing

trace or dashboard screenshot.
The label changes when the next

GUI update checks the age. That
distinction is the design

question. How long can a reading
sit still before stillness

begins to suggest confidence? A
rhythm is a choice about

attention. Latest packet state
gives someone a place to glance

for the most recent readings.
Those gauges do not preserve

every intermediate value. The
dashboard also keeps packet

counters and a recent arrival
rate view, a different kind of

evidence about the stream. A
quiet display and a detailed

record serve different kinds of
attention. A motor value, a

battery reading, and a brief
loss of contact need different

amounts of concern. More
frequent repainting cannot

decide which difference matters.
The interface has to give the

person a way to notice an
important change without making

every arrival demand a turn of
the head.

Let quiet mean something. The
next study would compare the

same readings under steady
delivery, a short gap, and an

extended silence. Ask what the
person believes the robot is

doing. Ask when they notice the
reading has become old. Keep the

stale condition visible while
they decide. There is a useful

kind of calm here. A display
that lets someone look away,

then return with a clear idea of
how much it still knows. You

have been listening to Moth and
Gravel Field Notes. The written
edition is at mothandgravel.com.
